newsitem.title: UK: Volcano quieter as Montserrat awaits evacuation.
newsitem.headline: Volcano quieter as Montserrat awaits evacuation.

text.p: Britain was on Tuesday hastily drawing up plans for a voluntary evacuation of the Caribbean island of Montserrat, whose rumbling volcano could explode in a new eruption at any moment.
Officials were meeting to decide detailed arrangements for those islanders who want to leave the dependent British territory and when exactly the evacuation can start.
Britain has already committed more than $66 million to disaster aid on Montserrat and a British warship, the HMS Liverpool, is anchored off the island to coordinate emergency help.
The Soufriere Hills volcano began hurling ash and rock into the air in July 1995, ending 400 years of dormancy.
Fresh eruptions this June left at least 19 people dead and earlier this month virtually destroyed the capital, Plymouth.
Most of the remaining 4,000 to 5,000 islanders who want to go will leave by ferries for nearby Antigua and other islands on the Leeward islands chain. Some may travel on to Britain.

The decision to hold a partial, voluntary evacuation was taken on Monday after scientists monitoring the volcano, in the south of the island, said the tremors could build to a new eruption and a huge explosion could not be ruled out.
The volcano was quieter on Tuesday but its threat remained undiminished.
"Right now it's behaving itself," said David Snelson, captain of HMS Liverpool.

"I think one could say that's part of the problem here...it can lull people into a false sense of security and all the time, underneath its cloud cover, it's actually growing," Snelson said in a telephone interview with BBC Radio.
Snelson said the major worry for the authorities was that even the former safe area in the north of the island could be damaged by any fresh eruption.
The danger zone was expanded northwards over the weekend to include Salem, the largest town still inhabited since Plymouth was abandoned.
But residents said there was little sense of panic on the island, known as the Emerald Isle both because of its lush vegetation and in homage to its Irish early settlers.
